Appendix C A Pattern Language for an Ostrom Game

This appendix retains the eighteen-pattern snapshot of the reported game experiment. It is distinct from the later twenty-four-member F11 find experiment and does not claim to validate the War Machine’s integrated run.

This appendix reports a small closed experiment carried out on a system we did not build. Snatch or Share is a multiplayer teaching game inspired by Elinor Ostrom’s work on institutions for collective action, distributed with five treatments that differ only in the institutional arrangement surrounding an identical exchange.https://github.com/AllianceBioversityCIAT/snatchgame. The collection was written from the game’s five mermaid design flowcharts, not from its client or server source. P1 holds ten tokens and P2 holds ten of another kind; a player’s own tokens score one and the other player’s score two, so acquiring is worth twice holding. Each round P1 abstains or proposes an offer naming what it gives and what it asks, and P2 accepts, refuses, or snatches — taking the offer and paying nothing. The treatments add, in turn, compulsory offers (G2), a symbolic mark (G3), an adjudicator that reverts and then inverts a theft (G4), and non-binding talk before the choice (G5).

The connection this rests on is Ostrom’s own. Asking whether institutional analysis has an underlying set of universal building blocks, she writes that “Christopher Alexander (1964) earlier conceptualized all components of social arrangements as having a pattern and being a unit. Units have subunits and are themselves parts of larger units that fit together as a pattern” (13, p. 11), citing Notes on the Synthesis of Form (2). Bringing a pattern collection to a game built on her work is therefore not an analogy imported from outside the subject.

The game is small enough to be understood completely and external enough that its outcomes are not ours to arrange. That combination is what makes it a test rather than an illustration: we can state what a pattern collection would have to do to be worth having, and then find out whether ours does it.

C.1. From pattern text to production rule

Moran read the pattern form as a production rule in 1971 (11), and observed that a cascade is a control problem: many patterns may apply at once, and one may enable or invalidate another. The compilation used here is his, with two disciplines added that the pattern form itself supplies.

The antecedent is if and however.

if names the situation; however names the counter-force that the then exists to overcome. Where that force is not live, the then would happen anyway and the pattern has nothing to contribute, so both conjuncts must hold before a pattern fires. The difference is not cosmetic. Exchange When Both Sides Gain fires on its if in every round in which a player holds tokens; its however — “attention to seizure risk can make abstention look like the objective” — restricts it to rounds where seizure is salient, so against a counterpart who has accepted four times in a row it correctly says nothing.

A guard may not mention the action taken this round.

A pattern advises a decision; conditioning its antecedent on that decision inverts the exercise and reports coverage that was never earned. Three guards in an earlier draft of this collection were written against whether P1 had already chosen to offer, and produced four phantom coverage gaps in G1 which disappeared when the policy, rather than the pattern, was made to decide.

A then the model cannot carry emits no action.

Four of the twelve play-grain patterns speak about the size of the ask, the talk channel, or a mark that changes no payoff — real features of the game that this harness does not represent. They remain advisory rather than being given an invented action, so that “not modelled” is recorded as itself.

The same test applies in both directions. Two of the seven acting patterns have a however that is live in every state where their if holds: “one acceptance is weak evidence, and a snatcher who accepts once has lost nothing by waiting” is a permanent condition of the game rather than a tension in the situation. A force that is never absent discriminates nothing, and is recorded as non-discriminating rather than given a guard that cannot fail.

C.2. Two policies over one collection

The resulting eighteen patterns — six about choosing an institution, twelve about playing within one — are exercised by two policies over identical scenarios. The first is grim trigger, the standard repeated-game strategy: offer until the counterpart defects once, then abstain for the rest of the game. It is hardcoded, and the collection cannot reach it. The second takes the patterns whose antecedent holds, orders them by precedence, acts on the first whose then yields an action, and records which pattern acted. Payoffs follow the game’s own stipulated rule; a denunciation under G4 is worth the two steps its pattern describes, the seized tokens restored and the asked-for tokens transferred at the defector’s expense.

G4 is the case the collection was written for. Grim trigger takes one loss and leaves; the pattern-driven policy denounces, has the transfer inverted, re-enters on the observed repair, and finishes +3 where grim finishes −1. Two patterns account for the entire difference, and a hardcoded policy could not consult either.

C.3. The wiring carries the score

futon2.aif.cascade-prior states that two cascades containing the same patterns but connecting them differently are different policies. Because precedence is data here, that claim can be run rather than asserted. The right-hand column of Table 4 promotes one pattern — Exchange When Both Sides Gain — above the remedy and the stop. Membership is unchanged, every pattern’s text is unchanged, and G4 moves from +3 to −5. What a collection scores is not a property of which patterns it contains.

This exposes something the pattern form does not carry. Beyond if, however and then there is the conflict-resolution order, and no pattern states it. The classical production-system answer is specificity — the rule with the most conjuncts wins — and it fails here: An Unmodelled Response Stops the Line has the fewest conjuncts of any acting pattern and has to be consulted first, because halting must dominate acting. That is a commitment about the collection rather than a property of any member of it, and there is nowhere in a pattern to record it. Its shape is the semilattice wiring that already distinguishes cascade identity in the implementation, which suggests the place for it is a collection-level record.

C.4. The cascade is a semilattice, not a chain

One pattern acts per round, so the sequence of acting patterns is linear. That sequence is not the cascade. The cascade is the sub-graph of @why authority edges that the acting patterns stand on, read from the pattern files at run time and closed upwards. For G4 against a snatcher it has seven nodes and ten edges (Figure 10), and four of those nodes stand on two authorities each.

That is Alexander’s own shape, and the point of A City Is Not a Tree (3): the overlap is the structure, and a hierarchy that forbids it loses what the overlap was doing. It is worth being precise about where the shape comes from. The authority edges were authored when the patterns were written; the harness reads them and adds nothing. What the run contributes is which part of the graph is reached.

Shape is therefore a property of the run, not of the collection. The same twelve patterns give a tree against a sharer — four nodes, three edges, no overlap, because the remedy structure is never engaged — and an overlapping structure under a remedy. A collection can support overlap and still produce trees indefinitely, if its situations never reach the shared authorities.

It is worth separating two properties that Alexander’s contrast runs together, because our own runs separate them. Overlap is the absence of the tree condition: some pattern stands on two authorities. Being a meet semilattice is the condition that any two patterns in the cascade have a greatest common authority. A rooted tree satisfies the second without the first, so “a semilattice rather than a tree” is a rhetorical contrast rather than a mathematical one. Checking both over the six runs gives all four combinations, which settles that they are independent axes rather than one axis named twice.

The G4 cascade is the one that is both: it carries overlap and every pair of its patterns has a greatest common authority, which is the structure Alexander’s argument is about. The G1 run against a snatcher fails the semilattice condition for a reason worth recording — Exchange When Both Sides Gain declares no authority at all, because it was written to state the game’s gain and had nothing above it to stand on, so a cascade containing it is disconnected and two of its patterns have no common authority to meet at. An orphan in the authority graph is visible here as a structural defect and is invisible in the pattern text.

Two further things are worth saying about what this measurement does and does not support. The counterpart’s disposition, holding the collection and the policy fixed, selects which sub-structure of the collection a run inhabits: the same twelve patterns produce four distinct shapes across six situations. And the one run that earns policy grade is also the one with the most overlap — but G2 against a snatcher carries overlap and is refused, so overlap is not sufficient, and with a single positive case nothing follows about necessity either.

C.5. What running it found that reading it did not

The collection was assessed by reading, which produced six gaps: nothing stated the gain that the whole exchange exists to realise, one treatment had no patterns at all, and so on. Those were repaired. A seventh gap appeared only on being run.

Against a snatcher under G1, the pattern-driven policy loses five where grim trigger loses one. After the first seizure nothing in the collection tells it to stop: Consult the Remedy Before Exiting presupposes that a remedy exists, G1 has none, and Exchange When Both Sides Gain continues to fire correctly on a situation where an exchange is genuinely available. The collection has no pattern for leaving an arrangement that offers no recourse — an omission which is invisible to a reader precisely because every individual pattern is right.

This is what the score is for. It does not measure whether a pattern is well written; it separates a collection that plays well from one that reads well, and those come apart.

C.6. Limits

The payoff asymmetry is the game’s stipulated teaching incentive and is adopted rather than derived. P2 is a fixed disposition rather than a chooser, so one pattern written for the responding player is excluded from the policy and its advice is untested; making P2 pattern-driven is the obvious next step. The size of the ask is a real feature of the game that this harness does not model, so the patterns about sizing an ask remain advisory. Precedence is authored by hand, and the six scenarios over five treatments and three dispositions form a space small enough to enumerate — a strength for auditing and a limit on generality.
